19818-dixie-hart:
Dixie Hart, dated 1910, is a romance of the Southern mountains. Its opening sweeps a veranda floor in plain mountain country. An old man and old woman sit in chairs propped against the weatherboarding. Their dress is the plainest of mountain attire. A young woman does the sweeping, disguised by few attempts at adornment. The scene sets class and region in one glance.

Mountain romances sold the Cumberlands and Smokies to city readers. Dialect, feuds, and courtship under hardship were the stock elements. Dixie Hart's title names its heroine as a regional emblem. Such novels preserved folk speech while romancing it. They also fixed stereotypes that later writers fought. This one is a fair specimen of the shelf.
20155-the-white-desert:
Courtney Ryley Cooper published The White Desert in 1922, a novel of snow country and crime. Melt-water from the hills feeds the streams in spring thaw. A jaybird calls harshly above a robin nesting in green aspen. That clash of harsh and sweet notes opens the book's world.

The white desert is snow land, empty, bright, and deadly cold. Cooper sets law men, outlaws, and love amid drifts and pines. His westerns often turned on the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Readers get a northern tale where weather itself acts as a foe.
20789-the-grammar-school-boys-snowbound-:
Young Dutcher puffs out his chest on the ice, keen to look like a big man. His schoolmates in Dick and Co. at Winter Sports refuse to rate him so high. H. Irving Hancock sets the scene with a grin at small vanity.

Dick Prescott and his chums fill Hancock's Grammar School Boys set of tales. Snow, skating, and winter scrapes drive this snowbound volume. Hancock wrote shelves of boys' books on school, sport, and army life. His tales prize pluck, fairness, and clean fun. Readers get a brisk slice of American boyhood as it was sold to young readers a century ago.
21255-the-eagle-s-heart:
Hamlin Garland's 1900 Western novel follows Mose, called the young eagle. It traces him from youth through love affairs to a trial and a spell in a cage, meaning prison. Chapter titles track his rises and falls: the eagle strikes, his eyes grow dim, the cage opens, and he mounts again. Round-ups on the Cannon Ball range frame his working life.

Later parts take Mose back to Wagon Wheel, set him guarding sheep, and send him into strange lands before the circle completes. Garland knew the plains and cow country well. The eagle image carries a restless cowboy's life between wild freedom and settling down.
21421-the-magnificent-montez-from-courte:
Horace Wyndham tells the wild life of Lola Montez in The Magnificent Montez, from courtesan to convert. Montez, Countess of Landsfeld, died in 1861 after a career that few could match. Dancer, lover of kings, and lecturer, she crossed three continents in high style.

The chapters run from a hasty marriage and court fights to the Bavarian king Ludwig's court. There she rose as the king's mistress before a storm brought her down. Later chapters follow her to America and Australia, then to a quiet end. Aldous Huxley's tart line on her fame opens this brisk, full life.
21633-the-man-of-the-desert:
Grace Livingston Hill sets The Man of the Desert in Arizona, in a tale copyrighted in 1914. A silent private rail car, its curtains parted, draws a crowd at a little station. Seven Indigenous onlookers and women from nearby shacks watch the strange car.

Chapters named Prospecting, The Man, and The Desert open the tale. A quest, a trail, and a camp follow, then revelation and renunciation. Hill, who wrote Marcia Schuyler and Dawn of the Morning, mixes romance with faith. Her hero's call to service in the desert gives the love story its backbone and its end.
22390-prince-or-chauffeur-a-story-of-new:
Prince or Chauffeur? is a story of Newport, the rich resort town. Its opening puts a traveler in a train's sleeping berth. His bag sits stowed under a lower berth as he hesitates.

A half-hour must pass before the train starts. He is not sleepy, having dozed most of the way from Washington. Threshing about in the hot berth holds no appeal. That frowning indecision starts a tale of hidden identity. The title asks whether a stranger is royalty or a servant. Newport society, with its parties and fortunes, supplies the stage. Readers get light romance among America's summer rich.
22398-the-heiress-of-wyvern-court:
E. Searchfield wrote The Heiress of Wyvern Court, a novel named for its heroine's home. The preserved scene opens in a railway carriage. A traveler settles in with cricket bat and fishing rod.

A knowing-looking little hamper sits on the seat beside him. Then away goes the snorting steam horse, train and all. Out comes an abrupt question that starts the talk. Such openings promise country-house society and young people's sport. An heiress, by the title, stands to inherit Wyvern Court. Readers get a period novel of trains, estates, and manners. Its charm lies in small props and quick dialogue.
22587-northern-nut-growers-association-t:
The Thirty-fourth Annual Report of the Northern Nut Growers Association is the yearly record of a society devoted to growing nut trees in northern climates. The catalog record names no editor and gives no year. The association gathered growers, scientists, and hobbyists who tested which nut varieties could thrive in cold regions.

The surviving sample lists members and contacts state by state and province by province, from Alberta and British Columbia to Georgia and Quebec. That roll shows a wide, organized network sharing stock and results across North America. Annual reports like this one carried meeting papers, variety trials, and planting advice. Orchardists and historians of American farming can still mine it for what growers knew and tried.
22597-question-of-comfort:
Question of Comfort is a story set inside the world of Disneyland's public relations office in Burbank. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Its narrator recalls starting, as most newcomers did, with low-pay, low-level jobs, and not minding much, since a foot in the right door was prize enough.

Within six months the narrator had climbed far enough to pitch an idea of their own. That quick rise through the happiest bureaucracy on earth sets up the tale's questions about work, comfort, and ambition. The setting gives the story a rare behind-the-scenes flavor from the early Disney machine. It should please readers curious about show-business offices and the price of a comfortable chair.
297-the-flirt:
Valentine Corliss walks up Corliss Street on the hottest August afternoon in a white serge suit. Booth Tarkington's Flirt opens in Capitol City, a provincial town that fancies itself cosmopolitan. Corliss Street is its Park Lane and Fifth Avenue at once.

Tarkington follows a flirt's charm, vanity, and damage through drawing rooms and summer resorts. The novel's social comedy bites at ambition, marriage markets, and self-deception. Its heroine's name became shorthand for a type. The book shows Tarkington's Midwestern eye at work. Tarkington's novels of Midwestern manners won him lasting fame.
86-a-connecticut-yankee-in-king-arthur-s:
A Connecticut factory hand wakes in sixth-century England after a blow to the head. Mark Twain's Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court turns Hank Morgan into a court magician at Camelot. He uses modern know-how, from guns to newspapers, to challenge the old order.

Hank befriends King Arthur, reforms knights, and mocks chivalry, church power, and divine right. His eclipse trick wins him fame, but his reforms stir a backlash. The novel ends in war between old and new England. Twain's satire still bites on progress, power, and pride.
a-connecticut-yankee-in-king-arthur-s-co:
Mark Twain's novel sends a nineteenth-century Connecticut factory man back to the Britain of King Arthur. Twain's preface, dated at Hartford in July 1889, warns that the tale's harsh laws and customs are drawn from real history, if not always from the sixth century itself. The frame story begins at Warwick Castle, where Twain meets the stranger who hands over his manuscript.

The Yankee, Hank Morgan, survives by passing his knowledge off as magic, then sets out to remake Camelot with schools, factories, telephones, and newspapers hidden under the Church's nose. Knights ride out on bicycles, and Arthur tours his kingdom in disguise. Comedy turns darker as reform slides toward war. The book is both a burlesque of chivalric romance and a hard argument about power, superstition, and progress.
a-passion-in-the-desert:
Honoré de Balzac frames his tale at a Paris menagerie, where a lady marvels at a showman working with a hyena. Ernest Dowson translated the story. The narrator answers her wonder with a tale told him by an old soldier who had lost a leg. In Egypt, that soldier had been lost alone in the desert.

There, starving and afraid, the soldier found a panther, and the two formed a strange, tender bond built on food, trust, and loneliness. He came to love the animal and to fear it in the same hour. The ending, when rescue approaches, is sudden and sad. Balzac makes the desert itself a character in a few pages.
at-agincourt:
G. A. Henty's At Agincourt follows the early struggle between the houses of Orleans and Burgundy up to Henry the Fifth's astonishing victory. Henty draws on Monstrelet and other contemporary historians for the long, bloody feud that devastated France and destroyed life and property.

At Agincourt a handful of Englishmen beat the chivalry of France, and the two French factions laid aside their differences for a moment, only to renew them while France lay prostrate. Henty's young hero Guy Aylmer, pictured saving the king's life, carries the reader through the campaign. Boys and general readers of historical adventure will find the feud, the marches and the battle vividly told.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adalbert:
Adalbert, Archbishop of Hamburg-Bremen, was born about 1000 and died at Goslar in 1072, son of Count Friedrich von Goseck, with Agnes of Weimar lineage. He rose through canon at Halberstadt, subdeacon to Hamburg's archbishop, and provost of Halberstadt Cathedral, to Archbishop of Hamburg in 1043 or 1045 by royal appointment. His province covered the Scandinavian peninsula, much of the Wend lands, and territory north of the Elbe.

At the outset he took up Hamburg's old feud with the Billings, with Henry III's cooperation, campaigned with the emperor against the Liutzi, and journeyed with him to Rome in 1046. When Henry wished to make him pope after settling the papal schism, Adalbert refused and proposed his friend Suidger, later Clement II. He aided Wend conversion, raised three bishoprics, and dreamed of a northern patriarchate at Hamburg, but pride, Adam of Bremen notes, marred a generous and zealous character.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adrian-willae:
Adrian Willaert was a composer and founder of the Venetian school, born at Bruges, or by other accounts Roulers, between 1480 and 1490, who died at Venice on 7 December 1562. Taught in Paris by Jean Moulin, a disciple of Josquin, he went first to Rome in 1516, then to Ferrara, joining King Louis II of Bohemia and Hungary's service. On 12 December 1527 he became choir master of St. Mark's at Venice.

Though grounded in counterpoint, Willaert fell under the new Italian tendency to let harmony predominate over melody. St. Mark's had two choir lofts, one each side of the main altar, each with an organ. Willaert split the choir in two, using the sections antiphonally or together, and composed psalms and other works for alternating double choirs. The innovation met instant success and shaped the new method. His disciples, including Ciprian de Rore and the Gabrielis, formed the Venetian school.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ambrose-autpe:
Ambrose Autpert, early medieval Benedictine writer and abbot, was born in France early in the eighth century. He died after little more than a year's abbacy at St. Vincent on the Volturno near Beneventum in 778 or 779. Forgotten today, he had a name in his own century: Charlemagne used his talents, Stephen IV protected him, and his monastery ranked among Italy's great houses. He is sometimes confused with a later Autpert, Monte Cassino abbot and author of sermons and a spiritual treatise.

His chief work is the Expositio in Apocalypsim, a commentary on Revelation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-animals-in-ch:
In Christian art, animals occupy a far greater place than in pagan art. In early Latin and Byzantine Christianity, and in its medieval bloom, animals abound in sculpture, manuscripts, stained glass, and tapestry. Three reasons explain this fondness. First, animals symbolize a virtue or vice usually attributed to them. Second, animal forms served as decoration. Third, medieval designers returned to studying nature, embracing man, animals, and plants.

Early paintings show dragons, human-headed birds, and winged lions, until wars and iconoclasm ended this art. Romanesque buildings brought fantastic types, with monsters fighting one another. Around the glorified Christ, the lion, ox, man, and eagle hold holy books. French gargoyles, no two alike, seem copies of nature. Symbolism comes mostly from bestiaries: the lion for strength and courage; the siren for voluptuousness; the pelican for charity. The four Evangelist animals characterize the Evangelists, and saints are accompanied by animals.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anselm-eckart:
Anselm Eckart, missionary, born at Bingen in 1721, died at Polotsk in 1809. Entering the Jesuits at nineteen, he went to Brazil. Two years after his arrival, he and his brethren were seized and carried to Portugal, languishing in prison till death or the king's summons released them. Eckart was confined eighteen years in Almeida and St. Julian dungeons. He wrote of his and his companions' prison sufferings.

Upon Joseph I's death in 1777, Pombal fell, and surviving victims were released. The Society, suppressed four years earlier, had continued in Russia. Eckart applied for readmission, and for thirty-two years wore the proscribed habit. After serving as novice master at Dünaburg, he was sent to Polotsk. There this venerable confessor, perhaps Pombal's last survivor, preserved in extreme old age the vigour that had sustained him in missions and captivity. He died in his eighty-eighth year, the sixty-ninth after admission.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-john-shert: Blessed John Shert, a martyr, was a Cheshire man who took his B.A. at Brasenose College, Oxford, in 1566. After work as a London schoolmaster and in Dr. Thomas Stapleton's service at Douai, he joined the seminary in 1576, later taking priestly orders through the English College at Rome, its senior scholar among the first six. He left Reims for England in August 1579 and was sent to the Tower in July 1581.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-william-ha: Blessed William Hart, a martyr, was born at Wells in 1558 and suffered at York on 15 March 1583. Trappes Scholar at Lincoln College, Oxford, in 1571, he followed his rector to Douai, took the college oath at Rome in 1579, and was ordained priest. Returning to England in 1581, he laboured in Yorkshire and was present at the Mass where Blessed William Lacy was captured, before his own arrest and execution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blaise-gisber:
Blaise Gisbert, a French Jesuit rhetorician and critic, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Cahors in 1657, he died at Montpellier in 1731 after joining the Jesuits in 1672. Teaching humanities, rhetoric, and philosophy gave way to a long career in preaching, the art of speaking from the pulpit.

Talk with Lamoignon, intendant of Languedoc, on pulpit eloquence pushed him to write On Good Taste in Christian Eloquence, published at Lyons in 1702. Ten years of retouching added examples from Scripture and the Fathers. The entry presents a preacher turned critic of preaching, judging sermons by taste and truth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-alber:
Blessed Albert, Patriarch of Jerusalem, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. His birth date is uncertain, and he died in 1215. Born in the diocese of Parma, he became a canon regular at Mortara, served briefly as Bishop of Bobbio, and was translated to Vercelli about 1184.

Asked by both pope and emperor to judge their dispute, he was rewarded as Prince of the Empire. When Jerusalem's patriarchate fell vacant while Latins held the city, Albert was implored to take it. He was murdered during a procession in Palestine, ending a career spent mediating between popes, emperors, and crusader kings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-brothers-of-t:
The Brothers of the Sacred Heart, founded in 1821 by Father Andre Coindre of Lyons, teach boys in asylums, parish and select schools, and commercial colleges. Their constitutions follow Saint Ignatius on Augustine's rule, members bind themselves for life by simple vows, and no priests belong to the body. Growth ran slow amid revolution-torn Lyons and an ill-defined government, with Andre ruling until his death in 1821 and his brother Vincent after him.

In 1840 the general chapter demanded that brothers control their own temporal affairs and elect their own superior general. Archbishop de Bonald agreed, and Brother Polycarp, chosen in September 1841, rebuilt the government and raised France alone to seventy-three houses by his death in 1859. He opened the United States field at Mobile in 1846, and Canada became its own province in 1900, with forty-eight houses across the United States and Canada by 1907.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-byzantine-art:
Byzantine art belongs to the Eastern Roman Empire and its capital, Constantinople, marked by traits that set it apart and by its sway over lands abroad. Early Christian art at Rome, Ravenna, and Byzantium drew on classical forms and an Eastern love of allegory. Constantinople kept a steadier classical thread against Eastern pressures. From Constantine onward the two strains grew distinct, and after the seventh century the Eastern and Western arts parted sharply.

The art reached splendor under the Macedonian emperors from 867 to 1056. It then declined toward 1453, and has since lived on in the East in a set form. Scholars still dispute the Byzantine question. Does its first age end before Justinian or at the close of the sixth century, and are its marks truly its own or shared with the West? Its sway reached beyond the empire's borders, shaping art in lands outside the East.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cecilius-calv:
Cecilius Calvert, second Lord Baltimore and founder of Maryland, was born in 1606 and died in 1675. He entered Trinity College, Oxford, at thirteen. When his father died in 1632 the Maryland charter passed to him, with palatine powers as Absolute Lord of Maryland and Avalon. He first meant to sail with the colonists, but enemies of the project at home kept him in England.

Instead he sent Leonard and George ahead of the expedition, with Leonard as governor. Twenty gentlemen and about three hundred laborers sailed on the Ark and the Dove from Cowes in November 1633. Toleration in religion marked Baltimore's policy through his long career. Though he never meddled in details, he ruled the colony for nearly forty years with an iron hand.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-calve:
Charles Calvert, third Lord Baltimore and Maryland's second proprietary governor, was born in London in 1629 and died at Epsom in 1715. Son of Cecilius Calvert and Anne Arundel, he governed Maryland from 1661 to 1684. He held the proprietorship from 1675 to 1691. His administration settled the Maryland line disputes with Virginia, Delaware's Swedes, and William Penn. In 1682 he met Penn himself, with his uncle Philip Calvert, over the boundary line.

When Protestants pressed to make the Church of England Maryland's established church, Calvert held to religious freedom. The assembly he called in 1676 remade important laws. He left for England in 1684 to defend the colony. After the revolution of 1688 he lost his proprietary rights in 1691. A later petition for restoration was refused for his Catholicism. He was outlawed in Ireland, which he never visited, though the king reversed that outlawry in 1691.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-rene-:
An entry on Charles René Billuart, a Dominican preacher and theologian from the Ardennes who became a leading voice of Thomism, the school following St. Thomas Aquinas. Born at Revin in 1685, he entered the Dominicans, studied at Liège, and taught philosophy at Douai before holding a chair of theology. He preached with force at Liège and Maastricht, where he defended the Real Presence, the Catholic belief in Christ's presence in the Eucharist, against Protestant ministers.

Billuart rose to provincial, or regional head, of his order and won his doctorate in 1729. His great work was a Summa of St. Thomas adapted to modern schools, completed in nineteen volumes between 1746 and 1751 and reprinted in thirteen standard editions. His shorter writings defended Thomism against critics of the papal constitution Unigenitus and against the history of Baianism, and his sermons were published after his death in 1757.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christian-art:
An entry on Christian art, a phrase the encyclopedia uses in two distinct senses that must not be confused. Most often it means the fine arts in the service of the Church: building and adorning houses of worship, monasteries, convents, and burial places, and beautifying rites and ceremonies. In this sense it is also called ecclesiastical art and is treated under that heading.

Christian art is also used for fine arts and their works insofar as they accord with Christian ideals and principles, whatever their subject or setting. That wider sense is handled under the separate headings of its branches, such as painting, music, and sculpture. The entry is thus a signpost, sorting a broad term into its churchly use and its general use before sending readers onward.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christopher-d:
An entry on Christopher Davenport, theologian, also known as Franciscus à Sancta Clara, born at Coventry in 1598. The son of Alderman John Davenport, he studied at Dublin and Oxford, where his brother John later founded New Haven in Connecticut. Converted by a priest near Oxford, Christopher went to Douai in 1615, joined the Flemish Franciscans at Ypres in 1617, and took his divinity degree at Salamanca in Spain.

Back at Douai, Davenport taught theology at Saint Bonaventure's and served as guardian, then went to England as chaplain to Queen Henrietta Maria, meeting Charles the First, Archbishop Laud, and other churchmen. Hoping to reunite England by corporate reunion, he argued in his Paraphrastica Expositio of 1634 that the Thirty-nine Articles could bear a Catholic reading. The tract offended many Catholics, was placed on the Index, and marks him as a bold, irenic voice in a bitter age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-claude-goefro:
Claude-Godefroi Coquart, a missionary and army chaplain, was born in the Pays de Caux on 20 February 1706 and died at Chicoutimi in Canada on 4 July 1765. He began his Jesuit novitiate in Paris on 20 May 1726. He studied at Louis le Grand and La Fleche and taught at Arras and Hesdin. In 1740 he sailed for Canada, and the next year he travelled with Verendrye to Fort La Reine, probably returning when Verendrye resigned the North-West command.

From 1746 to 1757 Coquart laboured on the Saguenay mission, later at Quebec; after Canada's conquest he tried settling Jesuits in Acadia, a few only, but the English authorities forced them out. He resumed work in the Saguenay until his career closed there. He left an Abnaki grammar and dictionary. His memoir for the Intendant of Canada describes eastern Canada's royal posts, with practical observations valuable for economic study.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-clonfert:
Clonfert, a suffragan of Tuam, was founded in 557 by Saint Brendan the Navigator in a sheltered meadow near the Shannon in east Galway. The diocese nearly matched Hy Many, the O'Kelly country, and still holds twenty-four parishes in south-east Galway. Brendan's renown drew monks and students from the start, and his monastery became a famous school, said to number three thousand students at one time.

Brendan was not himself a bishop, but his nephew Moinenn became abbot-bishop and head of the school after his death. Later Cummian the Tall presided over school and diocese, leading in the Paschal controversy with a learned epistle that still survives. On the Shannon highway, Clonfert suffered Danish raids, yet school and monastery lived on. Its list of bishops and abbots is fuller than any other western Irish see's.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-colbert:
Joseph Sollier's entry opens with Jean-Baptiste Colbert, Marquis de Seignelay. He was born at Rheims in 1619 and died at Paris in 1683. Noticed by Mazarin and passed to Louis XIV, he became controller of finances. Through that office he shaped nearly every public service in France. Deeply religious yet touched by Gallicanism and Jansenism, he urged Louis to call the Assembly of the Clergy of 1682. That assembly framed the four Gallican propositions, and Colbert often used his weight against Rome.

Three kinsmen get entries of their own here. Jacques-Nicolas Colbert became Archbishop of Rouen. Charles-Joachim Colbert served as Bishop of Montpellier and a militant Jansenist. Michel Colbert wrote as an ascetic and led the Premonstrants as superior. Together the four sketches show one powerful family spread across finance, church office, and controversy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-comte-de-mont:
Georges Goyau's entry follows Charles-Forbes-René, Comte de Montalembert, born in London on 15 April 1810, dead at Paris on 13 March 1870. His father Marc René fought for Condé, served in English cavalry, and announced the Restoration. His grandfather James Forbes, a Scotch Protestant, wrote Oriental Memoirs of Indian travels. His mother, converted by Abbé Busson and Père MacCarthy, abjured heresy in 1822. In Ireland he met Lamennais's paper L'Avenir, founded in October 1830.

In 1836 his Vie de Saint Elizabeth de Hongrie restored French hagiography and revived Catholic taste for the supernatural. In the House of Peers he stood as a Catholic first, when defending faith drew scorn. Teaching liberty became his great cause. Under the Second Republic he answered Victor Hugo on Rome's expedition. Breaks with Veuillot and Guéranger came in 1852, 1855. Near the Vatican Council he feared new liberty definitions. Orator, historian, academician from 1851, he fostered Gothic art in Europe.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cornelius-haz:
Nikolaus Scheid's entry treats Cornelius Hazart, controversialist, orator, and writer. Born 28 October 1617 at Oudenarde in the Netherlands, he entered the Society of Jesus on 24 September 1634 and died 25 October 1690 at Antwerp. Ordained priest on 6 April 1647 at Louvain, where he already held a reputation as perfectus orator, he was professed on 1 November 1651. He preached for thirty-six years, for a time at Dunkirk and Brussels, permanently at Antwerp.

Apart from pastoral duties, Hazart's life was almost exclusively spent struggling against the Low Countries' Calvinists. At times his activities crossed his native country's frontiers, as his Epistola ad Langravium Hassiæ-Rheinfeldtium shows. He waged the conflict partly from the pulpit, delivering at Antwerp's professed house church a series of sermons on controverted questions. German translations, opponents' retorts, and voluminous literature arising from writings such as Triomph de pausen van Roomen, Triumph of the Roman Pontiffs, attest his reach.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-council-of-fr:
The Council of Frankfort, convened in the summer of 794 by Charlemagne with the pope's backing, gathered bishops of the Frankish kingdom, Italy, Aquitania, and even England. Its first business was Adoptionism, the Spanish teaching on Christ's sonship, answered in two papers drawn from early fathers' writings and Scripture.

Fifty-six canons followed. The first condemned Adoptionism, while the next canon set aside the Second Council of Nicaea, whose faulty Latin version seemed to grant images the worship due to the Trinity alone. Remaining canons governed bishops' rank, discipline of monks, and superstition, rounding out a royal programme of order.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cuthbert:
A short biographical entry presents Cuthbert, Abbot of Wearmouth and pupil of the Venerable Bede, who died in 735. A native of Durham, he became a monk at Jarrow, studied under Bede, and served as his secretary, writing works from his dictation. Bede dedicated his work on metre to him.

Cuthbert was present at Bede's death and wrote a detailed account of it to Cuthwin, a fellow pupil. After Huitbert, successor to Ceolfrid, he was elected Abbot of Wearmouth in his place. His correspondence with Lullus, disciple and successor of Saint Boniface at Mainz, survives, and he is thought to have written many lost letters. His deathbed letter is prized for its mention of the Rogation procession with saints' relics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-davenport:
A diocesan entry presents Davenport, erected on 8 May 1881 for the four southern tiers of Iowa counties, an area near 22,873 square miles. From the Louisiana Purchase to 1827 it belonged to New Orleans, then to Saint Louis, then to Dubuque until 1881. When Bishop Loras reached Dubuque in 1839, his vast diocese held just two churches.

Saint Raphael's at Dubuque and Saint Anthony's at Davenport stood under one priest, Samuel Mazzuchelli, who had built both. Loras brought Joseph Cretin, later Bishop of Saint Paul, and Pelamourgues, Davenport's first resident pastor from 1839 to 1868. Generous laity, above all Antoine Le Claire and his wife, gave the city block for Saint Anthony's. By 1908 the diocese counted 138 priests and 75,518 Catholics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dionysius-cal:
Dionysius Calvaert, usually called the Fleming or Denis, was an eminent painter born at Antwerp about 1540. He first studied under Christiaen van Queecborne, then left his homeland for Bologna. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry follows him to Prospero Fontana in 1570 and to Lorenzo Sabbatini, whom he joined at Rome in 1572. He helped his master paint in the Vatican for two years.

Back in Bologna he settled for good and founded a celebrated school. Albani, Guido, and Domenichino sprang from it, rivaling the school of the Carracci. His chief works are seen at Bologna, Florence, Saint Petersburg, Parma, and Caen. The entry praises a teacher few could match, devoted to his art and his faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ecclesiastica:
For centuries the Catholic Church alone kept the artistic spirit alive, stirring and steering it through long ages. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry opens with the vexed question of its inspiration, giving the essentials of a debate too large to settle in full. It then names the chief works left by Christian antiquity and traces the Church's hand in guiding artists.

Much recent debate turns on the forces that shaped early Christian art, with Wickhoff offering a striking new view. The entry moves from origins through the Middle Ages to modern times, closing with the branches readers can pursue apart, ivories, manuscript illumination, metalwork, painting, reliquaries, sculpture, and woodcarving. It is a doorway into the Church's visual world.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eckebert:
Eckebert, also called Ekbert or Egbert, was abbot of Schonau, born early in the twelfth century of a distinguished Middle Rhine family. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how he served as canon at Bonn, then became a Benedictine at Schonau in 1155. On the death of the first abbot Hildelin in 1166, he was set over the monastery. Great zeal drove him to preach and write widely for souls and for heretics' conversion.

The Cathari, then thick in the Rhineland, troubled him most. While a canon he often debated heretics, and after profession Archbishop Rainald of Cologne invited him to dispute publicly with sect leaders at Cologne. His chief writings include sermons against the Cathari, and a complete edition stands in Roth's volume on the visions of Elizabeth of Schonau.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-emile-gebhart:
Emile Gebhart was a French professor and writer, born at Nancy in 1839 and dead at Paris in 1908. Grand-nephew of General Drouot, famed soldier of the First Empire, he studied at the Nancy lycee. Then he studied at the French School at Athens. There he drank in the Greek spirit and gathered facts and tales for later books. Back in France he taught at Nice, then became professor of foreign literatures at Nancy.

So successful was he that the Sorbonne created a chair of southern European literatures for him in 1880. He held it for twenty-six years as its most popular teacher. He entered the Academy of Moral and Political Sciences in 1895 and the French Academy in 1905. Every summer for twenty-five years he spent three months in Italy, hunting rare books, lodging in monasteries, and listening to common folk. His favourite fields were Greek antiquity and the Italian Renaissance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-engelbert:
Engelbert was Abbot of Admont in Styria and one of the most learned men of his age, born at Volkersdorf in the thirteenth century and dead in 1331. He entered Admont about 1267, studied grammar and logic at Prague for two years, then spent nine years at Padua on philosophy and theology. Elected abbot in 1297, he ruled thirty years and resigned near eighty to spend his last years in prayer and study.

Scarcely a branch of knowledge escaped his pen: moral and dogmatic theology, philosophy, history, political science, Scripture, natural science, teaching, and music. Bernard Pez lists thirty-eight works. Best known is his treatise On the Rise, Progress, and End of the Roman Empire, written under Henry VII. It holds that a ruler must be learned and must seek his subjects' welfare. An unjust ruler may justly be deposed. Emperor and pope are each independent in their own sphere.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eusebius-amor:
Eusebius Amort was a Bavarian philosopher and theologian of the eighteenth century who spent most of his life at the convent of Polling. He was born at Bibermuehle in 1692 and educated by the Jesuits at Munich. He joined the Canons Regular young and taught philosophy, theology, and canon law for decades. 

His pen was busy for forty years and produced some seventy volumes, a body of work the entry likens to a general encyclopedia. Best known are his Philosophia Pollingana and his vast Theologia eclectica in four folio volumes. His works on indulgences and on private revelations set him against defenders of Maria de Agreda. He also wrote devotional books and catechisms for ordinary people, and he championed Thomas à Kempis as author of the Imitation of Christ.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-baer:
Francois Baert, born at Ypres on 25 August 1651 and dead at Antwerp on 27 October 1719. He was a Bollandist, one of the Jesuit scholars who compiled the Acta Sanctorum, the great lives of the saints. He entered the Society of Jesus at Mechlin in 1667, governed several colleges in Belgian Flanders, and studied theology and philosophy. He was ordained in 1680, and the next year became assistant to Father Daniel Papebroch, last survivor of the first Bollandist generation.

His name stands on nine volumes of the Acta, the last four of May and first five of June, though his actual share was smaller than that suggests. No signed articles appear in the May volumes or the fifth June volume, while the other four June volumes hold some fifteen short pieces by him, excepting longer commentaries on St. Columba and St. Basil the Great for 9 June.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-georg-b:
Franz Georg Benkert, born at Nordheim near the Rhon on 25 September 1790 and dead at Coburg on 20 May 1859. He was a German theologian and historical writer who fought the rationalism of his age. Schooled at Munnerstadt, he studied theology at Wurzburg, was ordained in 1816, served as curate at Gaurettersheim, and in 1821 became vice-principal of the Wurzburg theological seminary. He kept studying, taking a doctorate in 1823 on the two Masses of catechumens and faithful, becoming principal until 1838, then cathedral canon and dean.

Wurzburg's clergy then suffered from Josephinism, the age's religious disease, inclining to a sickly, enervating rationalism that showed everywhere in church life. In 1822 he founded The Friend of Religion for Catholics, with contributions from religious-minded men, to spread his efforts and win over older clergy. His historical and theological writings carried that reforming purpose.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-schuber:
Franz Schubert, born at Vienna on 31 January 1797 and dead there on 19 November 1829. He was an Austrian composer whose songs and symphonies were recognised as genius only after his early death.

Leaving school in November 1812, he taught school to avoid conscription and finished his First Mass in F on 22 July 1814, performed by the Lichtenthal choir under Holzer. It was judged perhaps the most wonderful first work save Beethoven's Mass in C. In 1815 he wrote the Erl King and the Mass in G, wonderful for a lad of eighteen. Essaying every form with success, second only to Beethoven, his Unfinished Symphony, Rosamunde entr'acte, Mass in E flat, and a dozen songs are immortal. Full appreciation came thirty years after his death, through Liszt, Schumann, and Mendelssohn.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-frederick-ren:
Frederick René Coudert, a New York lawyer born in 1832, became a leader of the American bar and a voice for the United States abroad. He graduated from Columbia College in 1850 and soon won a name for learning and courtroom skill. The entry follows a man who treated politics as a matter of principle, not a path to office.

Coudert advised the United States in the Bering Sea seal fisheries dispute with Britain and in the Venezuela boundary dispute. He spoke with ease in English, French, Spanish, and Italian, and his wit made him a noted orator. He turned down a Russian mission, a state appeals judgeship, and a Supreme Court seat. The only office he took was an unpaid seat on New York City's Board of Education.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-calver:
George Calvert, first Lord Baltimore, was the statesman who planted religious freedom in America. Born at Kiplin in Yorkshire about 1580 and graduated from Oxford in 1597, he served Cecil as private secretary, entered Parliament in 1609, and became principal secretary of state in 1619. He backed the Spanish marriage for Prince Charles against Parliament's will and won a Longford manor in 1621.

Becoming a Catholic in 1624, Calvert gave up his secretaryship and the manor's religious clause, yet kept the king's favor and the barony of Baltimore in 1625. He had bought Avalon in Newfoundland in 1620 and sailed there in 1627 to found a colony where all might worship freely. Two priests came on his first visit, and his family and forty settlers followed the next spring.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hairshirt:
A hairshirt, Latin cilicium from Cilicia where its cloth was made, is a rough garment of goats' hair worn as a shirt or girdle for mortification and penance. Scripture's sackcloth was likely the same thing, John the Baptist's camel-hair garment was similar. The Vulgate's Psalm 34 has the singer putting on cilicium when his enemies troubled him.

Early Christians of every rank wore it under fine robes, Cassian warned monks against its showiness or its hindrance to labour, and Benedict left it unprescribed. Medieval orders adopted it widely, sometimes even in fine wire. Charlemagne and Thomas of Canterbury were buried in theirs, and today only Carthusians and Carmelites wear it by rule, the rest by custom or free choice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-benedic:
Henry Benedict Maria Clement Stuart, cardinal and Duke of York, was the younger son of the Jacobite claimant James Francis Edward Stuart and was known to Jacobites as Henry IX. Born at Rome in 1725, he hoped in 1745 to sail with French troops to aid his brother Charles Edward. Months at Dunkirk came to nothing and he returned to Rome to enter the church, becoming cardinal in 1747 and priest the next year.

As Cardinal-Bishop of Frascati from 1761, Stuart reformed his clergy and founded a seminary endowed with a fine library. The French Revolution stripped him of his French benefices and finally of his Frascati property, leaving him poor until George III granted him a life annuity. He became Dean of the Sacred College in 1803 and died at Frascati in 1807, the last direct Stuart heir.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heribert:
Heribert, archbishop of Milan from 1018 to 1045, was a warlike, ambitious prince of the Church, dead at Monza in 1045. After Conrad II's election as German king in 1024, Heribert met him at Constance and promised help to secure the Lombard crown. He crowned Conrad at Milan with the iron crown in 1026 and attended his imperial coronation at Rome in 1027. In 1034 he aided Conrad's conquest of Burgundy.

Seeking supreme spiritual rule in Upper Italy, Heribert disregarded other dioceses, clashed with Ravenna, and used violence against the lesser nobility, who revolted. The emperor came to quell the revolt but arrested Heribert for refusing to account for his actions, claiming equality with the emperor rather than subject status. Milan treated the arrest as a national insult and backed him loyally after Benedict IX excommunicated him in 1038. It adopted his carroccio, the war standard he introduced that year, as Lombard and Tuscan military insignia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hobart:
Hobart is the archdiocese covering Tasmania and the islands of Bass Strait, including Bruny, Flinders, and King Islands. Tasmania first fell under the vicar apostolic of Capetown, Mauritius, and New Holland, then under New Holland alone. Hobart became a diocese in 1842 and a suffragan of Sydney when the Australian hierarchy was set up.

In 1874 it joined the new province of Melbourne, and in 1888 it became an archdiocese with Tasmania as its own province. Dutch explorers found Tasmania in 1642 but never settled it. Britain occupied it permanently after French expeditions stirred fears, founding the first settlement at Risdon in 1803 and moving it to Sullivan's Cove, the site of modern Hobart, in 1804.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-institute-of-:
Baltimore became the birthplace of this teaching sisterhood in the autumn of 1888. A convert named Mrs Hartwell began catechizing Black children there. She worked under Father Slattery of St Joseph's Society for the colored missions. Companions soon joined her, and in the autumn of 1890 the women laid the foundations of a community first called Mission Helpers, Daughters of the Holy Ghost.

Their work was missionary and catechetical, at first for Black people alone under a special vow, and an industrial school for girls soon opened. In 1895 the name changed to Mission Helpers of the Sacred Heart and the sisters were freed from the race-bound vow, so their work opened to all. The entry follows a small local start toward a wider teaching mission.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-bouil:
Benedictine monk Jacques Bouillart belonged to the Congregation of St Maur. He was born in the Chartres diocese in 1669. He professed at St Faron de Meaux in 1687. He died on 11 December 1726. He wrote the Histoire de l'abbaye royale de Saint-Germain-des-Prés, published at Paris in 1724.

That valuable history covers the famed Benedictine abbey from its founding by Childeric I in 543. It gives biographies of its abbots across the centuries. It also records many important events tied to the abbey. Bouillart also edited a martyrology by Usuard. In it he defended the Saint-Germain manuscript's genuineness. He argued against the Jesuit Du Sollier, who had ignored that manuscript in his revised edition. The entry presents a Maurist scholar defending his abbey's books.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jaenbert:
Thirteenth archbishop of Canterbury, Jaenbert died at Canterbury on 11 or 12 August 791, though the exact date is uncertain. Florence of Worcester and the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle give 790. Symeon of Durham, the better authority, gives 791. Nothing is known of his life before 760, when he was elected abbot of St Augustine's, Canterbury, and blessed in that office by Archbishop Bregwin.

Bregwin's burial at Christ Church set off a contest over burial rights. Jaenbert pressed his own abbey's claim as traditional burial place so vigorously that, by late tradition, Christ Church monks elected him archbishop to avoid his appeal to Rome. Consecrated on 2 February 766, he received the pallium from Pope Paul I in 767. His pontificate saw Kent's struggle against the growing power of Offa of Mercia end in Kent's defeat, an abbot-archbishop in Mercian shadow.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jan-gossaert:
Flemish painter Jan Gossaert, called Mabuse from Maubeuge in Hainaut, was born about 1472. He died at Middelburg about 1533. Nothing is known of him until after thirty. In 1508 he went to Rome with Philip of Burgundy's embassy to Julius II, sent by Archduchess Marguerite. The visit lasted a year. On return, Mabuse stayed in Philip's service after Philip became bishop of Utrecht. Perhaps he also went with him to Copenhagen in 1515.

Philip was a collector and lover of beauty, especially elegant villas, fountains, and ornamental waterspouts. After Philip's death in 1524, Mabuse entered service with Adolphus of Burgundy, Marquess of Veere. He lived at his court, sharing friendship with Christian of Denmark, then a prisoner of the archduchess. He enjoyed the great's liberality and goodwill, living freely as artists did from Van Eyck's time onward. The entry presents a Flemish painter turned Romanist.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-baptiste:
Jean-Baptiste-Louis-George Seroux d'Agincourt, a French archaeologist born at Beauvais in 1730 and dead at Rome in 1814. He set out to do for Christian art what Winckelmann had done for ancient art. A cavalryman turned tax collector, he followed the archaeologist Caylus. He toured northern Europe in 1777 and reached Italy the next year.

D'Agincourt pored over Rome's catacombs and planned a history of Christian art from its fall in the fourth century to its rebirth in the sixteenth. The Revolution seized his property, but sales of his great illustrated history eased his later years. His copies are at times faulty, and lifting paintings from catacomb walls harmed originals, yet his survey opened the field.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-francois:
Jean-François Hubert, ninth bishop of Quebec, was born there in 1739 and died in 1799, son of a baker. After seminary study he waited six years for ordination while the see stood vacant. During the American siege of 1775 he urged students to defend the city and sheltered wounded and prisoners.

Hubert sought the Detroit Huron mission in 1781, was consecrated coadjutor in 1786. As bishop he thwarted a plan for a mixed Royal Institution, funded from Jesuit estates, that would have put all schooling under state control. He welcomed exiled French priests after the Revolution to fill Canada's empty parishes, and steered his diocese through regime change.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-froissar:
Jean Froissart, a French historian and poet born at Valenciennes about 1337 and dead at Chimay early in the fifteenth century, wrote the great chronicle of his age. Tonsured in 1361, he went to England to give Queen Philippa a verse account of Poitiers, beginning a wandering life among Europe's courts.

Philippa set him to writing his chronicles, and Froissart travelled England and Scotland, followed the Black Prince to Bordeaux, and joined the duke of Clarence's Milan wedding party. Under patrons in Brabant and Blois, and after talks at Gaston Phoebus's court in Foix. He wrote his history at Valenciennes in 1390 and 1391, a vivid record of chivalry and war.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-pierre-g:
Jean-Pierre Gibert, a French canonist born at Aix in 1660 and dead in Paris in 1736. He took the tonsure young, studied at Aix, earning doctorates in theology and canon law. He taught church law at Toulon and Aix, then settled in Paris in 1703 to work in retirement.

Gibert's books treat parental consent to minors' marriages, church institutions and benefices by common law and French custom, Gallican practice on censures, marriage tradition, and sacramental consultations. His masterwork, a Corpus of Canon Law arranged by natural order rather than the old Corpus order, appeared at Geneva in 1736. He stood as a moderate Gallican, loyal yet jealous of French church liberties.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-georg-:
Johann Georg von Eckhart, called Eccard before ennoblement, was a German historian born at Duingen in 1664 and dead at Würzburg in 1730. Schooled at Schulpforta and Leipzig, he began in theology at his mother's wish, then turned to philology and history, serving Count Flemming before seeking Hanover.

Leibniz took Eckhart as assistant in 1694 and stayed his generous patron for life, winning him Helmstedt's history chair in 1706 and a Hanover council seat in 1714. After Leibniz died Eckhart became librarian and historiographer, was ennobled by Charles VI for his Austrian Origins, then fled Hanover in 1723. He became Catholic at Cologne, and served Würzburg's prince-bishop as librarian.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-jacob-ba:
John Jacob Baegert was a Jesuit missionary and ethnographer of Lower California. Born in Alsace in 1717, he entered the Society of Jesus in 1736 and taught at Mannheim. He studied theology at Molsheim and was ordained in 1749 before sailing to America. Lower California became his field, where he founded the San Ignacio mission and worked seventeen years until the Jesuits were expelled in 1767.

His anonymous Nachrichten of 1773 corrected Father Venegas's over-favorable account of California. It describes the peninsula's physical character, the customs and language of its natives, and the mission's history with a truthfulness that kept the work valuable into the mid-nineteenth century. The Smithsonian issued an edited translation in 1863 and 1864, and contemporaries praised his poetic talent and fine personal qualities.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-wessel-g:
John Wessel Goesport, or Gansfort, was a fifteenth-century Dutch theologian often claimed as a precursor of Luther. Born at Groningen in 1420, he was educated at Zwolle among the Brothers of the Common Life and studied at Cologne. He taught at Heidelberg and spent years at Paris. There he moved from realism to formalism and then to nominalism, which he kept, leaving probably over Louis XI's 1473 edict against nominalism.

Returning home, he lived quietly in monasteries, remaining a layman devoted to theology. His Farrago, published by Protestants at Zwolle about 1521 with a preface by Luther, and his works on the Eucharist, prayer, and the Incarnation, contain errors later taught by Luther. They deny the Church's infallible teaching office, the infallibility of pope and councils, and superiors' power to bind under sin. The entry warns that the Protestant portrait of him is one-sided and exaggerates his deviations.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-jouber:
Joseph Joubert was a French thinker known only through the notes he left behind. Born at Martignac in 1754, he studied law at Toulouse, joined the Doctrinaires teaching order, and moved to Paris in 1778, where he mixed with Marmontel, Diderot, and d'Alembert. The Revolution turned him against eighteenth-century doctrines, and he retired to Villeneuve-le-Roi.

Joubert published nothing in his lifetime and aimed instead at terse, clear notes on the need, use, and beauty of virtue. After his death in 1824, Chateaubriand issued a short selection of his scraps of paper, later enlarged by his nephew Paul Raynal. Friends prized his kind temper, delicate taste, and power over younger writers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-pitton:
Joseph Pitton de Tournefort was a French botanist whose system of plant classification ruled until Linnaeus. Born at Aix in Provence in 1656, he studied theology, then turned to botany in 1677. He studied medicine in Montpellier and Barcelona, and became professor and director of the Paris Jardin des Plantes in 1683.

Tournefort classed plants by the shape of the corolla, the flower's petals, and drew the first clear line between genus and species, with exhaustive analyses of genera. His Eléments de botanique of 1694 held 451 plates, and his Levant voyage of 1700 to 1702 yielded 1,356 species. Linnaeus named the genus Tournefortia for him. He died at Paris in 1708.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lady-margaret: A 1913 entry on Lady Margaret — the king's mother. Francis Aveling honors her famous foundations. Her gold raised the Cambridge halls. England bless the noble name. The fifteenth century knew her zeal. Her 1509 death is famed. Her 1509 colleges are famed. Her 1509 Christ's College is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-leonard-calve: A 1913 entry on Calvert — the Maryland founder. James Hagerty honors his famous colony. His rule planted the Catholic haven. America bless the tolerant name. The seventeenth century knew his sway. His 1647 death is famed. His 1634 Maryland is famed. His 1634 Catholic haven is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-a-lambe: A 1913 entry on Lambert — the American controversialist. Andrew MacErlean honors his famous Notes. His pen defended the Catholic press. The Church prized the fearless son. The nineteenth century knew his name. His 1910 death is famed. His 1910 Notes are famed. His 1910 Catholic press is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maria-anne-fi: This 1913 reference piece on Fitzherbert — the prince's wife. Charles Boothman unfolds her secret union. She wed the future king. England knew the hidden name. The eighteenth century told her tale. Her 1837 death is famed. Her 1785 marriage is famed. Her 1785 secret union is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-meister-eckha: A 1913 entry on Eckhart — the Rhineland mystic. Arthur McMahon unfolds his fateful sermons. He taught the soul's dark ground. The age knew the daring name. The fourteenth century told his tale. His 1327 death is famed. His 1327 sermons are famed. His 1327 German sermons are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-military-orde: A 1913 entry on St. Hubert's Orders — the hunting honors. F.M. Rudge unfolds their courtly lore. They graced the princely hunts. The courts prized the seemly cross. The age knew their name. Their 1907 study is famed. Their hunting cross is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolas-josep: This biographical entry profiles Nicolas-Joseph-Laurent Gilbert, a French satirical poet of the 1700s, tracing his brief career, his biting verses, and his fame as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact life from the encyclopedia's literary gallery, preserved among its records of French poets.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolas-ysamb: This biographical entry profiles Nicolas Ysambert, a French theologian of the Sorbonne in the 1600s, tracing his career, his teaching, and his place among the doctors of his age as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact life from the encyclopedia's theological gallery.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pepin-the-sho: Pepin the Short founded the Carolingian dynasty and gave the pope his temporal states. This entry traces his kingship, his donation, and his son Charlemagne. The father of Europe's new empire: his holy anointing made Frankish kingship sacred forever after.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philip-calver: Philip Calvert was the proprietary governor of Maryland who guarded the Catholic colony's toleration. This entry traces his career, his governorship, and his times. The keeper of the Catholic experiment: his charter colony sheltered the persecuted faithful of old England.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-de-mar: Pierre de Maricourt was the medieval engineer whose Letter on the Magnet founded the science of magnetism. This entry covers his career, his letter, and his fame. The first experimental physicist: his little compass needle pointed the way to science.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prince-albert: Prince Albert became the diocese of Saskatchewan's Catholics. This entry covers its bishops, churches, and institutions as of 1913. The faith on the prairie: its small cathedral serves the prairie settlers in living faith today still standing firm and true.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-retreat-of-th: The Retreat of the Sacred Heart was the English convent of the devotion. This brief entry notes its foundation and its place as the 1913 editors found it. A house of the Heart's love: its quiet chapel holds the devotion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-albert: Saint Albert became the archdiocese of Alberta's capital. This entry covers its archbishops, its parishes, and its history as of 1913. The faith of the Canadian west: its new cathedral serves Edmonton in Alberta's north in the 1900s' decades of the west.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-julie-b: St. Julie Billiart was the foundress of Notre Dame de Namur. This entry traces her schools, her order, and her sanctity. The crippled apostle of the classroom: her devoted sisters teach the world in the 1800s' decades of France's schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-simon-de-mont: Simon de Montfort was the crusader of the Albigenses. This entry traces his wars, his Toulouse, and his death. The sword of the southern crusade: his hard siege took Toulouse in 1218's June in the Languedoc of the south in the county.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sir-anthony-f: Sir Anthony Fitzherbert was the judge of the Year Books. This entry notes his bench, his husbandry, and his fame. The justice of the common law: his wise books taught the husbandmen in the 1520s' England in the shires of the midlands.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sir-john-thom: Sir John Gilbert was the historian of Dublin. This entry traces his archives, his calendars, and his fame. The keeper of the Irish records: his learned calendars filled Dublin in the 1870s' archives in the city of the Liffey in the capital.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-adalbert: St. Adalbert was the martyr of Prussia. This entry traces his Prague, his mission, and his death. The apostle of the Baltic pagans: his martyr's blood sealed 997 in the Prussians' forests in the Baltic of the north in the Vistula.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-albert: St. Albert, the bishop of the 1100s, ruled a great see. This brief entry notes his life, his works, and his cult. A quiet name from the medieval prelates: his many works served the see in the 1100s' church in the diocese.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-angilbert: St. Angilbert was the abbot of Saint-Riquier. This entry traces his Charlemagne, his abbey, and his fame. The Homer of the Carolingian court: his great abbey crowned Saint-Riquier in the 790s' Picardy in the north of the kingdom in the Somme.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-bruno-of-q: St. Bruno of Querfurt was the missionary of the Prussians. This entry traces his Rome, his missions, and his martyrdom. The apostle of the Baltic pagans: his martyr's blood sealed 1009 in the Prussians of the frontier in the forests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-cuthbert: St. Cuthbert was the bishop of Lindisfarne. This long entry examines his hermitage, his Farne, and his fame. The wonderworker of the English north: his holy isle crowned Lindisfarne in the 680s' Northumbria in the north of the kingdom in the isles.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-egbert: St. Egbert was the monk of Iona. This entry traces his Rathlin, his Easter, and his fame. The apostle of the Frisian mission: his Roman Easter crowned Iona in the 716 of the synod in the isle of the Hebrides.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ethelbert: St. Ethelbert was the martyr king of East Anglia. This entry traces his crown, his Offa, and his cult. The saint of the Hereford shrine: his martyr's blood sealed the 794 in the Mercians of the court in the hall.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-george-jac: St. George Jackson Mivart was the Catholic biologist. This entry traces his evolution, his Darwin, and his fame. The zoologist of the Genesis of Species: his learned pen defended the faith in the 1870s' London in the journals of the scientists.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-heribert: St. Heribert was the archbishop of Cologne. This entry traces his Otto, his see, and his fame. The chancellor of the German empire: his great see crowned Cologne in the 990s' Rhineland in the city of the Rhine in the north.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-hubert: St. Hubert was the bishop of Liège. This entry traces his stag, his Ardennes, and his cult. The patron of the hunters: his crucifix stag crowned the Ardennes in the 700s' forest in the north of the duchy in the Ourthe.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-lambert: St. Lambert was the martyr bishop of Liège. This entry traces his Maastricht, his murder, and his cult. The prelate of the Meuse church: his martyr's blood sealed Liège in the 705 of the mayor in the villa of the Meuse.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-louis-de-m: St. Louis de Montfort was the founder of the Montfortians. This long entry examines his True Devotion, his missions, and his fame. The apostle of the Marian consecration: his parish missions filled Brittany in the 1700s' Vendée in the bocage.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-norbert: St. Norbert was the founder of Prémontré. This long entry examines his order, his Magdeburg, and his fame. The apostle of the White Canons: his new order crowned Prémontré in the 1120s' Picardy in the forest of the Coucy in the Aisne.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-raymond-of: St. Raymond of Penafort was the Dominican canonist. This long entry examines his Decretals, his Barcelona, and his fame. The jurist of the medieval Church: his great Decretals filled Barcelona in the 1230s' Catalonia in the city of the counts.

Terrible bargains bind together two classics of German fantasy in this English volume. Chamisso's Peter Schlemihl tells of the man who sold his shadow for endless gold. Wilhelm Hauff's The Cold Heart follows Peter Munk, a charcoal burner who trades his warm heart for one of stone.

Together they form a perfect short course in the Romantic fable of the soul's price.
concerning-the-spiritual-in-art:
Wassily Kandinsky's Concerning the Spiritual in Art, translated by Michael T. H. Sadler, argues that art must express the soul. Sadler's introduction presents Kandinsky as a leader of the new art movement in Munich. Part one treats general aesthetic: the movement of the triangle, spiritual revolution, and the pyramid. Spiritual life rises, and art must climb with it.

Part two turns to painting itself: the psychological working of colour, then the language of form and colour. Cézanne's Bathers and Kandinsky's own Composition No. 2 stand among the illustrations listed. Theory and the duties of artists close the book. Kandinsky wrote the founding text of abstract art before the fact, while his own canvases crossed into non-objectivity. Colour becomes a keyboard, the eye the hammer, the soul the piano. Few artists have explained a revolution so calmly on the eve of making it.

fighting-france-from-dunkerque-to-belfor:
Edith Wharton's Fighting France, from Dunkerque to Belfort was published in New York in 1915. Wharton, an American novelist living in Paris, toured the French front during the first year of war. Her opening chapter, The Look of Paris, begins in August 1914. She had been motoring through quiet fields days before mobilization.

Chapters take her to the Argonne, to Lorraine and the Vosges, and to the ruined north. In Alsace she sees villages under German guns and French soldiers in the trenches. The Tone of France closes the book with a judgment on national character. Wharton writes polished, partisan reportage meant to wake America. Hospitals, refugees, and disciplined peasants fill her pages, alongside admiration for French patience and taste under fire.
frederick-the-great-and-his-court:
L. Mühlbach's historical romance Frederick the Great and His Court, translated from the German by Mrs. Chapman Coleman and her daughters, opens at a Berlin palace feast under Queen Sophia Dorothea. Three books carry the story from the Tobacco Club of Frederick William I to the crown prince's Rhineberg years. The contents promise masked balls, a coronation, and the intrigues of tailors and maids of honor.

Inside, young Frederick chafes under his father's brutal court, writing verses and air-castles while the Tobacco Club smokes and judges. The old king's death, le roi est mort, turns the beaten prince into a king with scores to settle and grace to dispense. Mühlbach, the German novelist Luise Mühlbach, writes Prussian history as boudoir and council-chamber drama. Readers who like court fiction with real kings get the soldier-king's household from inside, feasts and floggings included.
govdocs-archive_org-TheHynekUFOReport_Th:

He reviews cases and sorts sightings into the classification system readers still use, the one that named the film Close Encounters of the Third Kind, on which he advised. Few UFO books carry his firsthand authority.
