govdocs-archive_org-protocols-of-learned:
The Protocols of the Learned Elders of Zion is a fabricated text, first spread in Russia in the early 1900s. It pretends to record a Jewish plot for world control. In fact it was forged, borrowing from older fiction and satire, and it has been exposed as a fake many times.

The forgery did real harm, feeding antisemitic movements for more than a century. The library keeps it as an archive holding for the study of its history and its debunking, without backing of any kind. Read as evidence about propaganda and hate, it shows how a lie, once printed, can outlive every proof against it.
govdocs-archive_org-the-lords-work-and-t: The Lords' Work and the Lords of the Earth is an antisemitic tract claiming that Zionists are seizing world power. It is presented here as an archive holding, without endorsement. Documents of hate are kept for research, so that scholars can trace how such charges were built and spread. Readers meet the tract as evidence about its authors and their era, not as a claim the library asks anyone to believe.
govdocs-archive_org-the-pleiades-title-p: Arthur de Gobineau wrote The Pleiades as a novel of ideas, and it opens with a travel journal. Gobineau, a French aristocrat and diplomat, is better known for his infamous essay on race. The novel lets him argue through characters instead: young Europeans talk, travel, and test their beliefs about art, love, and society. It stands as a classic of nineteenth-century French literature and a window into its author's mind.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_foia-int:
Newly released JFK files include minutes from the small groups that ran America's covert operations under President Kennedy. Arturo Jimenez-Bacardi and Peter Kornbluh edited this briefing book, number 890, published in April 2025. The records come from the Special Group and the President's Foreign Intelligence Advisory Board.

Top secret briefings describe clandestine operations in Brazil, Chile, British Guiana, Haiti, Italy, Japan, and the Congo. That list alone shows how global Kennedy-era covert action was. Meeting minutes are valuable because they record decisions as they were made, by the officials who made them, before outcomes were known.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_intellig:
In the 1970s a Senate committee led by Frank Church investigated American intelligence abuses. Its report on CIA efforts to assassinate foreign leaders caused a major scandal. This briefing book revisits that report fifty years later.

The Church Committee's findings prompted new legal restraints on targeted killings by the United States. Before the report, assassination plots were discussed inside government as a policy tool. After it, they were formally banned, a line later administrations have tested but not openly erased. The posting preserves the scandal's documentary core and explains why its rules still get cited whenever targeted killing returns to debate.

How does a covert operation actually get approved in Washington? John Prados and Arturo Jimenez-Bacardi edited this briefing book, posted in March 2019, on that machinery during the Cold War. It covers both covert and overt CIA operations and how each was proposed.

The posting treats covert action as one element of the forward edge of American power. Proposal and approval paper shows the chain of signatures behind operations that were meant to stay deniable. For readers of case histories, this is the missing middle: not the operation itself, but the bureaucratic path an idea traveled before agents ever moved.

Law requires the CIA to notify Congress about covert actions, but how much it must tell was fought over in the 1980s. This briefing book, posted in February 2019, reviews declassified materials on that fight. Attorney General nominee William P. Barr figured prominently in it.

Barr had argued for limiting the CIA's duty to notify Congress. The question mattered after Iran-Contra, when lawmakers learned of operations late or never. The posting appeared as Barr faced confirmation hearings, which gave old legal memos new political weight. It shows notification rules as a real battleground over who watches the watchers.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-: Britain built its own atomic bomb after the war, partly because the United States had cut off the wartime partnership that helped create it. This briefing-book page is the first part of an Archive set on the British bomb and its American relationship. The evidence supplied here is the title alone, and the documents in this part are not described. The subject frames a long story: two allies who invented the weapon together, then spent decades negotiating how much of it to share.
grace-harlowe-s-overland-riders-on-the-g:
Jessie Graham Flower's Grace Harlowe's Overland Riders on the Great American Desert opens with cowboys laughing. Grace picks out the ponies for the desert journey and chooses an outlaw bronco. The guide Hi Lang doubts she can stick on him. She fights the vicious horse and wins the plainsmen's admiration.

The contents run as chapter synopses: a runaway bronco, a fainting conqueror, and Ping Wing the cook making discoveries. The Overland girls ride into the great silence, are shot at by a mountain mystery, and defend their water hole. Grace Harlowe leads her party of girls across the desert with a lasso as her diploma. Flower writes the series' formula at full gallop: competence, courage, and housekeeping under canvas. The desert tests the Overlanders as boarding school never could, and Grace's horsemanship answers every test first.
harriot-briefe-true-report:
Thomas Harriot was a scientist in Sir Walter Raleigh's service in the 1580s. His Briefe and True Report of Virginia appeared in 1590 in English. He had sailed to Roanoke and studied the Algonquian peoples at close range.

Harriot describes Native towns, crops, faith, and daily work with care. His report aimed to draw English backers to the new colony. De Bry's famed prints later spread his account across Europe in pictures. The book stands as the first English study of Algonquian peoples. It also marks the founding written record of English America itself. Harriot's clear eye gives the account its lasting worth.
hopes-and-fears-for-art:
William Morris, the designer, poet, and socialist craftsman, delivered the five lectures in Hopes and Fears for Art to working audiences. Longmans issued the pocket edition in 1919, from a text first published in 1882. Morris argues that the lesser arts, meaning decoration and craft, shape daily happiness. When machine production cheapens them, he warns, joy in labor dies with beauty.

The Lesser Arts opens by joining architecture, painting, and craft into one family. The Art of the People ties decoration to fair conditions for its makers. The Beauty of Life praises homes, towns, and workshops built for use and pleasure. Making the Best of It tells householders how to furnish honestly inside a flawed system. Prospects of Architecture in Civilisation closes by asking what building a juster age might raise. Students and craft revival readers still mine Morris here for doctrine: art thrives when work stays human and glad.
lectures-on-art:
Washington Allston's Lectures on Art appeared in 1850, after his death. Richard Henry Dana Jr. edited the volume. Friends had planned a larger work with his biography and letters.

Delays held that bigger project back for years. Meanwhile, readers kept calling for Allston's poems and prose. This volume answers those calls with his art lectures. Allston was a leading American painter of the Romantic age. His lectures treat beauty, taste, and the painter's craft with a poet's feeling. Dana, his editor, was a noted author himself. Their friendship helped preserve Allston's thought for American art.
little-alice-s-palace-or-the-sunny-heart:
T. Nelson and Sons published this children's story in London in 1872. Little Alice watches spring rain from a brown cottage window. Green blades spring up to catch the falling shower drops. They seem to laugh and sing with new life.

Alice talks to the grass as if it were siblings. No one else nearby can hear and answer her love. The tale's subtitle calls her heart a sunny one. Her palace grows from imagination inside a lonely country cottage. Grass blades bathed in the shower and made themselves clean. Spring came after a long, dreary winter to the cottage.
louis-lambert:
Louis Lambert is a novel by Honoré de Balzac, told by a schoolmate of its hero. Louis was born at Montoire, where his father owned a small tannery. At five he was reading the Old and New Testaments with hunger. His bent for study soon took him far beyond the family trade.

The boy begs books from all over the town and devours them. His mind turns to deep questions of spirit, will, and thought. Balzac shows a genius burning too bright for the body that holds it. The tale grows sad as Lambert's powers turn inward and break him. It is one of Balzac's most personal and searching works.
luther-s-little-instruction-book-the-sma:
Luther's Little Instruction Book is the Small Catechism of Martin Luther. Robert E. Smith translated this text from the German of the Triglot Concordia. That Lutheran book of confessions was printed at St. Louis in 1921. The catechism itself dates from 1529, in the Reformation's first years.

It teaches the faith 'the simple way a father should present it.' The Ten Commandments come first, each with a short 'What does this mean?' Then follow the Creed, the Lord's Prayer, and the sacraments. Luther's words are plain enough for children to learn by heart. The Little Instruction Book has taught Lutheran homes for five centuries. Few short books have shaped so many lives.
nasa-tm-19630012120-satellite-situation-:
Goddard Space Flight Center issued this satellite situation report on January 2, 1962. Data came from Goddard, NORAD, and the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory. The report lists every object then in orbit around Earth. Each entry gives launch date, period, tilt, and high and low points.

Explorer I, America's first satellite, heads the table of 1958 launches. Rocket bodies are listed beside the craft they lifted. Vanguard I still shows a live transmitting frequency in the table. Moon probes like Lunik I and Pioneer IV appear as heliocentric cases. The report is a dated census of the young space age, six years after Sputnik.
nasa-tm-19640002493-satellite-situation-: This satellite situation report belongs to NASA's running census of objects in orbit. Reports in the series were compiled by Goddard Space Flight Center with NORAD and the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory. They list satellites and debris with launch dates and orbital facts. The hosted sample preserves only garbled table data with no readable text, so this issue's date and contents cannot be described from the sample itself.
nasa-tm-19670027063-the-global-radiation:
Ehrhard Raschke and Musa Pasternak, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, wrote this paper in August 1967. It derives the global radiation balance of the Earth-atmosphere system, the account comparing sunlight absorbed against heat radiated back to space. Their data came from the meteorological satellite Nimbus II, which measured radiation over the whole globe from orbit.

For about two and a half months in 1966, the satellite's scanning radiometer recorded reflected solar radiation and emitted thermal radiation. Turning those readings into surface fluxes took empirical integration methods and corrections for how reflectivity changes with viewing angle. The corrections drew on balloon, aircraft, and satellite data. Results were computed for five half-month periods. The paper presents global maps for early June 1966 showing albedo, absorbed sunlight, emitted heat, and the balance itself. Averaged worldwide, the balance sat near zero, indicating a system nearly in radiative equilibrium.
nasa-tm-19680000600-radar-analysis-repor:
Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland issued this radar analysis report on January 30, 1967. It was approved by the Advanced Techniques Office of the Manned Flight Engineering Branch. The catalog record describes its focus: checking radar data captured on fast magnetic tape during spacecraft tracking.

The contents show an introduction, a history section, and a data analysis summary. Three appendices carry the working material. They hold radar analysis charts and running averages of the analysis. A third appendix covers standardization and analysis of radar digital magnetic tapes. The report preserves how tracking radar data was checked and cleaned.
nasa-tm-19690010415-a-theory-of-thermosp:
H. Volland wrote part one of a theory of thermospheric dynamics, a Goddard preprint numbered X-621-68-563 and dated December 1968. The thermosphere is the hot, thin upper layer where satellites drag against traces of air. Since the first satellite flew in 1957, drag readings had revealed how its density swells and shrinks over time.

Volland sorts those changes into regular effects and sporadic ones. Regular rhythms include the daily cycle, the Sun's rotation period, a half-year wave, and the eleven-year solar cycle. Sporadic effects include great air waves and the shocks of magnetic activity. Part one builds theory for the daily and solar cycle changes, the two rhythms his title names.
nasa-tm-19690027362-solution-of-lambert-:
E. R. Lancaster of Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this preprint, numbered X-643-69-310, on solving Lambert's problem for short arcs. Lambert's problem is a classic of trajectory design. Given two points in space and a travel time between them, find the orbit that connects them. Short arcs, where the craft barely moves along its path, defeat many standard solution methods.

Lancaster finds approximation formulas for the quantities the boundary conditions fix. He then develops a polynomial approximation built on those formulas. A numerical example drawn from two-body motion tests the approach in practice. Closing remarks weigh where the short arc method stands. The note is brief, technical, and aimed at orbit computers who meet this stubborn case.
nasa-tm-19710003598-apollo-13-mission-re:
The Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston issued this mission report, number MSC-02680, for Apollo 13. The flight had been planned as a landing in the Fra Mauro region of the Moon. An explosion on the way out turned it into a fight for survival instead.

About fifty-six hours into the flight, a fire in an oxygen tank crippled the service module. The landing was called off at once. The crew moved into the lunar module, which kept them alive on the long loop around the Moon and back. This report is the official account of the mission, its failure, and the rescue that followed.
nasa-tm-19710027929-apollo-14-mission-5-:
The Mission Evaluation Team at the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston prepared this five day report on Apollo 14. Apollo 14 lifted off at 21:03:02 Greenwich time on January 31, 1971. It was the third crewed landing mission, following the Apollo 13 failure. The report rests on a first review of early flight data. All event times inside count from that liftoff second.

The catalog record lists the report's ground. It covers the preflight experiments, the launch, and the moonwalks on the surface. Recovery of the crew and capsule closes the account. Five day reports gave managers a fast, shared picture of mission health. Later, fuller reports would replace these early findings.
nature-and-art:
Mrs Inchbald wrote Nature and Art, a novel reprinted here in an 1886 Cassell edition from London. An introduction before the story gives her own life in detail. Elizabeth Simpson was born in 1753 near Bury St Edmunds, one of eight children of a poor farmer.

That life story tells how she fled to London at about nineteen and sought stage work. A speech flaw had blocked her first try at Norwich. In London she wed Mr Inchbald, an actor who had courted her at home. Knowing her hard start helps frame the novel that follows, where nature and art stand as rival guides to life.
on-the-antiquity-of-the-chemical-art:
James Mactear gave this address on December 8, 1879. He spoke as president to the chemical section. Mactear asks how old the chemical art really is. Scholars had traced chemistry back to Geber, he notes. Geber lived in or about the year 778.

Professor Ferguson had written on eleven centuries of chemistry. Rodwell argued that alchemy began in Arabia then. No good proof showed an older origin, Mactear reports. Earlier chemists whom Geber named remain unknown to us. The address weighs claims for Egypt and other lands. It shows how historians of science test old traditions.
on-the-significance-of-science-and-art:
Leo Tolstoy wrote this essay for his book What to Do. This text was transcribed from the 1887 Crowell edition. Chapter one attacks the learned defense of idleness. Learned men claim science justifies who toils and who rests. Division of labor, they say, makes some command and others obey.

Tolstoy calls that doctrine a false justification of privilege. He recalls older claims that all that exists is reasonable. Rousseau, Lessing, and Spinoza offered other wisdom, he notes. No single thinker's wisdom should rule the crowd, he argues. The essay asks what knowledge is truly for.
peg-o-my-heart:
J. Hartley Manners wrote Peg O' My Heart as both a stage comedy and a novel. His preface, dated December 1922, counts the play's career with pride. It had been performed more than 8,000 times in the United States and Canada and 6,000 times in Britain and Ireland, with companies touring the world and a film in release.

The heroine, Peg, is a lively Irish girl who comes into an English fortune and unsettles the stiff household that receives her. The novel version sold over 194,000 copies in America alone. Manners's preface shows a modest comedy becoming an international theatrical phenomenon.
petty-troubles-of-married-life-first-par:
The first part of Balzac's Petty Troubles of Married Life begins with a preface he promises everyone will recognize. A friend describes a young woman: good family, well bred, pretty, and three hundred thousand francs of her own. Courtship follows in brisk dialogue, then the pecuniary question, two hideous notaries, the magistrate, the church, and the bridal chamber.

Then, Balzac asks, what? A crowd of petty unforeseen troubles. This first part collects the vexations husbands suffer, in scenes of dialogue and commentary. It is Balzac the anatomist, dissecting marriage one small irritation at a time.
petty-troubles-of-married-life-second-pa:
The second part of Balzac's Petty Troubles of Married Life opens with a preface about the colour of books. Books, he says, are dark or fair and have a sex, and he hopes his has one. The troubles so far, he admits, were inflicted by wives on husbands, and indignant women readers have been heard.

So this part turns the book around and gives the wife's side of the yoke. Marriage, he calls it, is a necessary, sacred, useful institution, often tight about the joints and sometimes too loose. The paired volumes make a complete comedy of conjugal grievance, fairly divided.
reminiscences-of-pioneer-days-in-st-paul:
Frank Moore gathered these pieces from articles written for the Daily Pioneer Press, recalling pioneer days in St. Paul. The first piece treats the struggles of early newspapers there. Moore imagines James M. Goodhue, the city's first editor, touring modern offices and marveling at the changes.

A web press turning out 25,000 impressions an hour replaces the hand press of 240, he notes. The linotype sets thousands of ems where a hand compositor set hundreds. Moore then turns to 1857, when Minnesota chose delegates to a convention on statehood. The vote ran so close that Republicans and Democrats met apart, and the Pioneer and the Minnesotian split the printing contract.
second-shetland-truck-system-report: William Guthrie stands as author of a report on the truck system in Shetland. Under that system, workers took goods instead of cash for their labor. The pages at hand carry only the publisher's header for the electronic edition. That header gives the title, the author's name, and issue data for the file. No text from the report itself appears here. Its findings and witness accounts stay unseen. For that reason, the scope and verdict of Guthrie's inquiry cannot be stated from what is shown.
seneca-minor-dialogues-stewart:
Seneca, the Roman Stoic who advised Emperor Nero, wrote the essays gathered here as his Minor Dialogues around the middle of the first century AD. Aubrey Stewart's English translation presents them from Project Gutenberg. The short works cover the questions a busy Roman of rank could not escape.

The essays treat anger and how to master it, mercy in rulers, the shortness of life, and the calm of a wise mind. Seneca writes as a man of the world, not a hermit: he knows courts, money, and grief from inside. His counsel is crisp and quotable. These essays are the easiest door into Roman Stoicism.
seneca-on-benefits-stewart:
Seneca's On Benefits, written around 60 AD, is his longest single work on the giving and receiving of favors. Aubrey Stewart's English translation is the text here. Roman life ran on favors exchanged; Seneca sets out the moral code behind the traffic.

Across seven books he asks when to give, how to give, and what thanks are owed in return. A benefit, he argues, lies in the giver's intent, not in the thing handed over. Ingratitude he counts the ugliest of vices, since it breaks the bonds holding society together. The book is a Stoic guide to generosity, favor, and debt of the heart.
seven-discourses-on-art:
Sir Joshua Reynolds delivered these seven addresses on art at the Royal Academy, at the schools' opening and at yearly prize meetings. Cassell's 1901 printing carries an opening essay on their worth. The essay ties the Academy's founding to these talks with fond pride.

Reynolds lays down rules of art from the view of a working genius: seek whole truths, not small accidents of detail. The essay pairs him with Boileau in French letters, who likewise prized good sense and plain strength. Students of painting get the founding doctrine of British art teaching, stated by its first great master.
sir-robert-hart:
Juliet Bredon, Sir Robert Hart's niece, told the romance of his great career in this biography, here in a second edition of 1910. Contents open with his early years and first years in China at Ningpo. The Allied Commission and Sir Harry Parkes figure in those consular days before Hart resigned that service.

Later chapters trace the birth of the Imperial Chinese Customs and Hart's rise to inspector general. Meetings with Chinese Gordon, a move to Peking, marriage, and the Burlingame mission follow. A family voice tells how an Ulsterman came to run China's customs and stand trusted at its court for decades.
speeches-from-the-dock-or-protests-of-ir:
Speeches from the Dock, Part I, or Protests of Irish Patriotism, gathers speeches given after conviction by Irish patriots. The title page names Theobald Wolfe Tone, William Orr, the brothers Sheares, and Robert Emmet. John Martin of 1848, William Smith O'Brien, Thomas Francis Meagher, Terence Bellew McManus, John Mitchel, and others follow. A. M. Sullivan printed the Dublin book in 1868, under a motto on freedom's battle passed from bleeding sire to son.

The text opens on the state of Ireland in early 1794. An agent of the French government had come to learn how far the Irish folk would go with France in a war on England. He was the Rev. William Jackson, an Irish Protestant clergyman who had lived some years away. From that probe, the book moves toward the trials and last words of the men on its title page.
starr-of-the-desert: B. M. Bower, author of Chip of the Flying U, wrote Starr, of the Desert, dated 1917. The contents open with A Commonplace Man Was Peter, then a chapter where Peter finds a way out, and Vic Should Worry. Later heads name a grease spot in the sand, Darn Such a Country, Holman Sommers the scientist, and the trail of Silvertown cords. Starr finds something in a secret room in Chapter XII, and Helen May sighs for romance in the next.
studies-and-essays-censorship-and-art:
John Galsworthy's Essays on Censorship and Art holds two pieces, About Censorship and Vague Thoughts on Art, under a motto from Anatole France warning that excess is always an evil. The first piece takes up the one censorship then standing in Britain, the censorship of plays.

Galsworthy writes with dry irony. The play censor works with smooth swiftness. He allows no public fuss and no appeal. He has the warm backing of the majority. So why not extend so fine a protector to all institutions? The mock praise exposes the cost of letting one man's conscience guard a nation's stage. The second essay turns from law to the making and judging of art itself.
tales-for-fifteen-or-imagination-and-hea: Only the front pages of an old electronic text are present here. They name the work Tales for Fifteen, or Imagination and Heart. They credit James Fenimore Cooper as author. He wrote under the pseudonym Jane Morgan. A transcriber's note adds a further fact. The text was made from a facsimile of the original edition. C. Wiley printed that edition at New York in 1823. It ran to a few pages over two hundred. No title page, contents, or tale text from the book itself appears in these pages.
the-clicking-of-cuthbert:
P. G. Wodehouse published these golf tales in 1922, under a dedication of comic solemnity. He honors John Henrie and Pat Rogie, jailed at Edinburgh in 1593 for playing gowff on the Links of Leith on the Sabbath. Robert Robertson, who got it in the neck for the same reason in 1604, joins the roll.

A foreword, signed Fore!, calls the book an epoch in his career and says it is written in blood. The author poses as a desperate man, an eighteen-handicap golfer who must look sharp or slip back into the twenties. He jokes that farce writers need a miserable private life, since the public likes its humorists piquantly unhappy. Till now, he claims, a cheerful nature has handicapped him in that trade. Wodehouse frames a set of golf stories as the cry of a seared soul, which is itself the first joke.
the-efficiency-expert:
The Efficiency Expert opens with Jimmy Torrance Jr. stepping into a college ring to fight for the boxing crown. Jimmy has captained the football team and stars at first base; a win this night would crown four fine years. His foe is a freshman of dark repute, whispered to be a paid pro in the fight game.

No author's name appears in these opening pages. Once out of school, Jimmy will hunt work and find his fame as a fixer of failing shops. The tale mixes sport, jobs, and graft in the brisk pulp style of its age.
the-flirt:
Booth Tarkington wrote The Flirt as a novel of a small city's best street and the folk who live on it. Valentine Corliss walks home at the start after years away.

Corliss Street bears his grandfather's name and ranks as the town's Fifth Avenue. On the hottest day of August, Corliss notes how the calm old street has changed: gasoline cars, wild new house styles, and a restless air. Tarkington draws a home town caught between old pride and new wealth, where a famed flirt holds court and a returned son must find his place again.
the-green-flag-and-other-stories-of-war-:
Arthur Conan Doyle wrote The Green Flag and Other Stories of War and Sport. A contents list names eleven tales. They are The Green Flag and Captain Sharkey. They are The Croxley Master and The Lord of Chateau Noir. They are The Striped Chest, The King of the Foxes, and The New Catacomb. They are The Debut of Bimbashi Joyce and A Foreign Office Romance.

The title tale opens in Ireland. Jack Conolly, of the Irish Shotgun Brigade, has been shot by Sergeant Murdoch of the constabulary. Jack's twin brother Dennis then joined the British Army. The countryside had become too hot for him. He lacked the seventy-five shillings that might have carried him to America. The sergeant whisked him off to the depot at Fermoy. Within weeks he joined the Royal Mallows. It was the darkest hour of the land struggle.
the-heart-of-the-desert-kut-le-of-the-de: Honore Willsie wrote The Heart of the Desert, also titled Kut-Le of the Desert, published in New York in 1913 with a frontispiece in colors by V. Herbert Dunton. Willsie is named as the author of Still Jim. The contents list chapters such as The Valley of the Pecos, The Caucasian Way, The Indian Way, The Pursuit, Entering the Desert Kindergarten, and Adrift in the Desert. The pages present go no further than the front matter.
the-illustrious-gaudissart:
Honoré de Balzac devoted this short novel to a traveling salesman. Felix Gaudissart is his hero. Katharine Prescott Wormeley translated the tale into English. Balzac opens with praise mixed with mockery. The commercial traveler was unknown to old times. He is a striking figure of the modern age. He carries ideas as stagecoaches carry men. He scatters light from the capital. Drowsy country regions receive it from his hands.

The portrait sharpens into comedy. Gaudissart is a scholar without learning. He is an unbelieving priest of the goods he sells. Paris has soaked him in its vices. The provinces still find him a jolly fellow. He knows men and places by name only. Things he sees at the surface. He measures the world with his own little tape-line. The tale sends this prince of talk into the country. He thinks he owns that ground already.
the-joyful-heart: Robert Haven Schauffler published this book of essays in 1914. Houghton Mifflin of Boston and New York issued it. An epigraph from Jean Finot fronts it. People who are nobly happy form the state's power, it declares. They are its beauty and its foundation too. Only the title pages and contents are present here. The essays themselves do not appear. The contents promise a defense of joy. The brimming cup, enthusiasm, and the auto-comrade follow. Vim and vision, printed joy, and the joyful heart for poets close the list.
the-lady-of-the-barge-the-lady-of-the-ba:
W. W. Jacobs opens the title story aboard the barge Arabella. Her master sits in the stern with his arm on the tiller. A religious argument with a schooner's mate has run aground. The skipper argued warmly for his mother's Seventh-day Baptist tenets. He nearly convinced himself he had inherited them. The mate defended an alarming Wesleyanism. He sealed the quarrel by calling the skipper a bargee.

The long summer day gives place to night. The skipper wonders where his mate Ted has got to. Ted is also his brother-in-law. He checks his worn silver watch. It says ten o'clock. Ted descends the ladder at that moment. It will be eleven in an hour's time, Ted observes. He asks to speak in private. A voice from the schooner urges him to fire away. Jacobs's Thames watermen talk his plots into motion.
the-lamp-in-the-desert: Ethel M. Dell published this novel in 1919. D. C. Hutchinson drew its illustration. A man kneels beside a woman there, arms around her in comfort. She dedicated the book to her dearly loved Elizabeth. It honors Elizabeth's goodness when she walked in the desert with her. A line from Psalm seventy-eight stands with it. It tells of being led all night with a light of fire. Only the title and dedication pages are present here. The story itself does not appear.
the-madonna-in-art: Estelle M. Hurll wrote The Madonna in Art, published in Boston by L. C. Page and Company in 1898 under an 1897 copyright. Its frontispiece is a photogravure of Giorgione's Madonna of Castelfranco. Only the title page and contents are present, so the chapters do not appear. The chapters sort her images by type: the portrait Madonna, the Madonna enthroned, the Madonna in the sky, and the pastoral Madonna. The Madonna in a home setting, the Madonna of love, and the Madonna in adoration follow.
the-man-in-court: Frederic Dewitt Wells, a justice of the Municipal Court of New York City, wrote The Man in Court, published by G. P. Putnam's Sons in 1917. Only the title page, dedication, and the start of the contents are present here, so the chapters themselves do not appear. The contents shown open with an introduction, then A Night Court at page 3 and The Civil Court at page 21. The Judge follows at page 39, promising a judge's own tour of the courts an ordinary person meets.
the-master-of-appleby-a-novel-tale-conce:
Francis Lynde's The Master of Appleby, copyrighted in 1902, concerns itself in part with the great struggle in the two Carolinas. Its subtitle promises that it deals chiefly with two gentlemen who loved one and the same lady. T. de Thulstrup supplied the illustrations. Lynde dedicated the book to Edward G. Richmond of Chattanooga, Tennessee, thanking him for kindness and encouragement.

The contents open with a narrator who whets his father's sword, then knits up some broken ends. Those chapter headings promise a tale told in retrospect, with old scores to settle. The Revolutionary struggle in the Carolinas supplies battles, loyalties, and divided families. Against that public war runs the private rivalry of two men bound to one woman. Readers get historical adventure in which the sword and the love story advance together, each sharpening the other.
the-pool-in-the-desert:
Sara Jeanette Duncan's The Pool in the Desert collects four stories: A Mother in India, An Impossible Ideal, The Hesitation of Miss Anderson, and the title piece. The first story is told by a soldier's wife whose husband, John, held a company when they married. Money was always short. They went without puddings to pay uniform bills, did his facings herself, and painted their own dog-cart.

A fat spider of a money-lender tempted them on their veranda, and John threatened to hand him over to the police. When daughter Cecily came, with a swamping burst of expense, the couple kept up a pretence of delight while the station pitied them. John walked the veranda with the baby until two in the morning. The narrator lay awake fearing a scorpion might drop on her. Their dread was of falling short of mankind's ideal standard.
the-public-vs-m-gustave-flaubert:
Prosecuting attorney M. Ernest Pinard addresses the court in the trial of Gustave Flaubert over Madame Bovary, serialized in the Revue de Paris in 1856. Pinard opens by admitting that charges of offending public morals and religion are vague terms that need careful handling before a jury.

Pinard explains his method for a long novel that cannot be read aloud in full. He will summarize the whole story, then point to the passages he calls incriminating, then answer objections to that approach. Readers get a clear view of how a nineteenth-century obscenity case was argued, with the title and its subtitle on provincial morals treated as clues to the author's intent.
the-quirt: B. M. Bower's western novel is presented with a list of her earlier books, from Good Indian and Lonesome Land through Flying U and Lazy A titles, Starr of the Desert, and Skyrider. A frontispiece caption describes Al's gun speaking as Warfield slumps to the ground, pointing to violence late in the story. Only the title pages and list of earlier works are present here, so the ranch narrative itself does not appear.
the-rim-of-the-desert: Ada Woodruff Anderson published her Northwest novel in 1915. Monte Crews supplied the frontispiece. She dedicated the book to her mother's memory. Her mother was her gentlest and kindest critic. Contents open with a man who never came back. A question and a broken axle follow in Snoqualmie Pass. Apples of Eden and a mountain road night come next. Columbia dunes close the opening list of chapters. Only the title pages and dedication are present here. The opening chapter list appears with them. The desert story itself does not appear.
the-rising-of-the-court:
Henry Lawson opens with a verse asking singers and judges where the meeting will be when human laws are nothing and spirits are free. His prose, the only kind kept in these pages, then enters a dingy courtroom deep and dim like a well.

Lawson describes the bench as a gingerbread throne, the witness box where poor people are bullied by petty lawyers, and a weary magistrate facing the same miserable scene. Women and men fill divided dock sections, drunk, trembling, or conscience-stricken over small thefts. Australian court reporting becomes social criticism with a poet's eye for light in a dark room.
the-secret-places-of-the-heart:
H. G. Wells published The Secret Places of the Heart in 1922. Its contents list only nine chapters. The consultation opens the book, and Lady Hardy follows. A departure, Maidenhead, and the land of the forgotten peoples come next. An encounter at Stonehenge and full moon precede the last days of Sir Richmond Hardy.

Chapter one places a visitor in Dr. Martineau's waiting room. The maid is a young woman of great natural calmness, Wells writes. She is used to annoyed visitors with too many umbrellas. She relieves this gentleman of his umbrella almost imperceptibly. She juggles his hat and coat onto a mahogany stand. When she asks his name, he gives it reluctantly. Hardy, he says, and the consultation begins.
the-secrets-of-the-great-city-a-work-des:
Edward Winslow Martin's The Secrets of the Great City promises to describe New York's virtues and vices. Its subtitle adds the city's mysteries, miseries, and crimes. Chapter one treats the city of New York itself. Martin calls it the largest and most important city in America. Its limits embrace all of Manhattan Island, he writes. The Hudson, East, and Harlem rivers bound it.

The island runs fifteen miles long and about a mile and a half wide, Martin says. The city lies at the head of New York Bay, within sight of the ocean. The Dutch settled it toward the close of 1614 and called it New Amsterdam, he recounts. In 1664 it passed to the English and took the name New York. The first settlement stood at the present Battery, behind a strong stockade. Its founders bought the island from the red men at a fair price, Martin claims.
the-turquoise-cup-and-the-desert:
Arthur Cosslett Smith's Turquoise Cup, published in 1903 with a companion tale, The Desert, opens on a cardinal archbishop's shaded balcony. The small cardinal clasps his well-kept hands on his breast. He stretches his feet so straight that a pigeon on the rail can see six inches of scarlet silk stocking. From there he watches two pigeons quarrel. His white hair and rebellious forehead lock make him resemble the first Napoleon before fame and fat. The pigeon's mate coquettes among the treetops, proves her liberty, tires of it, and returns.

The cardinal tells the pigeons there are days they make him regret not being 'of the world.' He adds that this is not one of them. Smith opens his tale with a churchman's amused detachment. The turquoise cup itself, and the Bedouin girl Khadija, wait inside.
un-doc-mehliss-report:
Detlev Mehlis, a German prosecutor, led the United Nations inquiry into the murder of Rafik Hariri, Lebanon's former prime minister. Hariri died in a huge truck bombing in Beirut in February 2005. The Security Council set up the inquiry soon after, and Mehlis delivered this report later that year.

The report lays out the evidence the team had gathered about the bombing plot. It points to links between the killers and Syrian and Lebanese security circles. Its findings raised pressure on Syria and shaped the push for a special court to try the case.
